records.issue_text: Tests only compare Prisma.Sql objects structurally via toEqual and never execute ANY(...) fragments, so the potential ANY() SQL breakage is invisible to the test suite
records.rationale: The updated tests for org/team authorization conditions assert equality on `Prisma.sql` objects that contain `ANY(...)` fragments (e.g. `expect(conditions).toEqual(Prisma.sql`(("teamId" = ANY(${[...] })) ... )`)`) but do not actually execute those SQL snippets against the DB in those cases. The only execution added is in `getBaseConditions` test via `$queryRaw` (`WHERE ${baseConditions}`), and that scenario uses `scope: "user"` with simple comparisons (no `ANY`). So a runtime SQL issue specific to `ANY(${array})` could pass this suite undetected.

records.issue_text: Org-scope condition inlines very large userId arrays as ANY(...) bind parameters with no cap; should use a subquery to avoid parameter limits and per-request recomputation (also applies to teamIds and userIdsFromTeam)
records.rationale: In this diff, org/team authorization is changed to raw SQL using array parameters: `Prisma.sql`("teamId" = ANY(${teamIds}))...`` and `("userId" = ANY(${uniqueUserIds}))...` in `buildOrgAuthorizationCondition`, and similarly `ANY(${userIdsFromTeam})` in `buildTeamAuthorizationCondition`. There is no cap/guard on the size of `teamIds`, `userIdsFromOrg`, or `userIdsFromTeam`, so very large orgs/teams could lead to oversized array bind payloads and avoidable per-request computation compared to using a subquery/join against memberships/teams.
records.stripped_text: Org-scope condition inlines very large userId arrays as ANY(...) bind parameters with no cap; should use a subquery to avoid parameter limits and per-request recomputation (also applies to teamIds and userIdsFromTeam)

records.issue_text: teamIds array not guarded against being empty before interpolation into ANY(), causing Postgres type-inference error and a thrown 500 instead of an empty result
records.rationale: In `buildOrgAuthorizationCondition`, `teamIds` is derived from `teamsFromOrg.map((t) => t.id)` and can be an empty array when an org has no teams. The new SQL condition unconditionally interpolates it into `Prisma.sql` as `("teamId" = ANY(${teamIds})) AND ("isTeamBooking" = true)`. Passing an empty array parameter into `ANY($1)` commonly triggers a Postgres type inference error (cannot determine type of empty array), which would throw instead of returning no rows. There is no guard for `teamIds.length === 0` before using `ANY()`, so this is a real defect introduced by the diff.
records.stripped_text: teamIds array not guarded against being empty before interpolation into ANY(), causing Postgres type-inference error and a thrown 500 instead of an empty result

records.issue_text: buildAuthorizationConditions silently returns NOTHING_CONDITION for an invalid scope instead of rejecting input, where the previous Zod parse would have thrown
records.rationale: The diff still defines `insightsBookingServiceOptionsSchema` as a Zod `discriminatedUnion("scope", ...)` over only `"user" | "org" | "team"` (see `insightsBookingServiceOptionsSchema = z.discriminatedUnion("scope", [...] )`). That means an invalid `scope` would be rejected at parse-time rather than reaching `buildAuthorizationConditions`. While `buildAuthorizationConditions` has an `else` fallback returning `NOTHING_CONDITION`, the finding’s claim that the change removed Zod rejection and now “silently” returns NOTHING for invalid scope is not supported by what’s shown in the diff.

records.issue_text: getBaseConditions fallback to 1=0 (NOTHING_CONDITION) when both conditions are null conflates 'no restrictions' with 'deny' and masks future logic errors
records.rationale: The finding hinges on the case where “both conditions are null”, but in this diff `authConditions` cannot be null: `async getAuthorizationConditions(): Promise<Prisma.Sql>` and `async buildAuthorizationConditions(): Promise<Prisma.Sql>` always return a `Prisma.Sql` (falling back to `const NOTHING_CONDITION = Prisma.sql`1=0``). Only `getFilterConditions()` can return `null`. Therefore the `else { return NOTHING_CONDITION; }` branch for “both null” in `getBaseConditions()` is effectively unreachable given the shown types/returns, so the described conflation doesn’t occur based on this diff.
